analysis.one_liner: Requires beef processors and grinders to test ground beef trimmings for E. coli O157:H7.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Federal Meat Inspection Act to require slaughterhouses, processing plants, and grinding facilities to test for E. coli O157:H7 at each step where beef trimmings are produced, received, or ground into ground beef [S2][S3]. Large plants — those handling more than 25,000 pounds of trim per day — would have to comply within 180 days, with smaller facilities covered after three years [S3]. Lots testing positive would have to be destroyed or treated before sale, results reported to the USDA within 24 hours, and plants with repeated positive results listed publicly as habitual violators [S3]. Imported trimmings would have to meet the same testing requirements, with domestic facilities running secondary tests to verify foreign certifications [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of ground beef, especially children, who face the greatest risk from E. coli O157:H7, a pathogen that can cause kidney failure and death. The bill would catch contaminated trimmings before they are ground and mixed, when a single tainted lot can spread through millions of pounds of burgers sold to households and restaurants.

how_it_helps.text: Requires testing for E. coli O157:H7 at the slaughterhouse or processing plant where trim is produced and again at the receiving facility before lots are combined, closing a gap where contamination discovered at final grinding is hard to trace back to its source [S3].

Requires that contaminated lots be disposed of or treated to eradicate the pathogen before entering commerce, and that positive results be reported to the Secretary of Agriculture electronically within 24 hours [S3].
Subjects imported trim, bench trim, and ground beef to the same testing rules as domestic product, with secondary testing by domestic facilities to verify foreign compliance [S2][S3].

Requires testing to be done by independent laboratories that establishments may not fire for reporting positive results, and plants with repeated positive tests would be publicly listed as habitual violators on the USDA website [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Beef slaughterhouses, processing plants, and grinding facilities would pay for testing, contract laboratories, and destroyed or treated product. The heaviest costs would fall on large operations producing more than 25,000 pounds of trim per day, which must comply within 180 days [S3]. Some of that cost would likely reach consumers through higher ground beef prices.

drawbacks.text: The costs fall almost entirely on the industry: each establishment must contract with an independent testing facility annually, run proficiency services, and destroy or treat entire contaminated lots of up to 2,000 pounds each, expenses that would likely be passed into ground beef prices [S3].

The 25,000-pounds-per-day threshold and 2,000-pound lot cap concentrate compliance work on large processors and could push smaller competitors toward consolidation, since the smallest plants get a three-year delay before coverage [S3].

Testing detects contamination but does not prevent it; outbreaks could still occur at steps the sampling plans do not capture, and industry could meet the letter of the rule through how it defines its sampling lots, subject only to USDA approval [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a tested pathogen-control step in a product that killed and hospitalized American children in the years before this bill, at a cost of routine testing and occasional destroyed product borne by processors and partly passed to shoppers. Food-safety testing of this kind is the mechanism the industry itself uses to catch contamination today; the objection is that the mandate is uniform and rigid rather than risk-based. On balance, the consumer protection is substantial and the compliance cost is modest relative to the cost of recalls, lawsuits, and illness.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the E. Coli Eradication Act of 2009 on November 18, 2009, with one Democratic cosponsor joining her [S1][S4][S5].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry; no further action of any kind appears in the record [S5].
The bill remained in committee with no hearing, markup, or vote for the remainder of the 111th Congress, which ended January 3, 2011 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Beef processors and grinding facilities are better off because the bill never advanced: they avoided mandatory independent testing, lot-size limits, 24-hour reporting of positive results, and public listing as habitual violators. Consumers of ground beef did not get the added testing, and imported trimmings remained subject to no parallel verification requirements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Beef processors, who avoided mandatory testing

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.role: U.S. Senator from New York; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on November 18, 2009.

for.name: 1 of 58 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only additional Senate support it attracted.

against.name: Chair, Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Beef processing industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory E. coli testing of beef trimmings during the 2009 food-safety debates, when major news reporting documented industry resistance to testing components destined for ground beef; the record shows no industry support for the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no voting record exists; its only demonstrated support was a Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, and the Democratic-controlled committee did not act on it.

industries.note: The bill would have required independent testing of every lot of trim, destruction or treatment of contaminated lots, 24-hour reporting of positives, and public listing of habitual violators, all at the industry's expense. Consumers would gain a safety check at the step where contamination is hardest to trace.
Every covered establishment would have to contract annually with an independent testing facility using methods equivalent to USDA's, creating steady demand for accredited labs.

industries.industry: Beef importers and foreign meat suppliers
industries.note: Imported trim and ground beef would have to meet the same testing rules as domestic product, with domestic facilities running secondary tests to verify foreign certifications, closing a loophole that otherwise lets untested trim enter the ground beef supply.
